background: Second-shift operations supervisor at a logistics distribution center near Joliet for about seven years, promoted from the floor. Ran a two-dozen-person crew until he was fired in January 2026, weeks after reporting unpaid off-the-clock work and blocked fire exits.
personality: Conscientious and detail-minded, proud of a spotless record, uneasy about looking like a complainer. Loyal to his old crew.
emotional_state: Anxious and financially frightened as the family's main earner; stung by the sudden turn against him after years of good reviews.
communication_style: Answers factual questions in plain, orderly terms and likes to walk through timelines. Goes quiet or minimizes when a topic could reflect on him.

objectives: Get his job back or fair back and front pay
Recover the unpaid off-the-clock wages for his crew
Walk away with a neutral reference
fears: Being branded a troublemaker and blackballed across regional logistics
Losing the house while out of work and without health coverage
Something small he did being twisted to justify the firing

volunteered.text: The timing is the whole thing — they wrote me up three weeks after I called the state hotline and fired me a couple months later. That's not a coincidence.
I put it in writing to HR — an email to Bethany Croll about the unpaid time and the blocked fire exits.
They terminated me on January 9th and said it was the performance plan plus a headcount reduction.

revealed_if_asked.text: My crew was working past clock-out all through last fall to hit the outbound numbers, and the new system stopped paying them for it.
When HR didn't really do anything, I called a state wage-and-safety hotline and got a confirmation number.
They put me on a performance improvement plan in December — first bad thing in my file in seven years.
What I want is my job back, or fair back pay, the unpaid wages, and a reference that isn't poison.

rapport_gated.text: Honestly? What keeps me up is that these site managers all know each other. If I get labeled the guy who sued, I'm done in this business.
I kept a notebook — every night we ran late, who stayed, how long. I haven't shown it to anybody. I wasn't sure if I was supposed to.

There's one thing. Last August I okayed a fifteen-minute timecard fix for one of my people because the system shorted him. It was outside policy, technically. I'm scared they'll use it to say I was the problem.

concealed.text: Back in October I quietly applied to one other logistics outfit and didn't get it. I haven't told anyone — it looks like I was already trying to leave, and I'm embarrassed about it.

unknown.text: I don't know whether that arbitration clause I signed, or the part that says no class actions, even holds up. That's why I need you.

knowledge_boundary.unknown_response_style: I don't remember the exact details on that / I'm not sure, I'd only be guessing.
color_topics: his long commute on the Metra line into work
